text: Some apocryphal tales claim that a humble miner with no artistic training, overtaken with patriotic spirit, was compelled to create the golden figure of George Washington astride a horse that stands proudly in our state capitol. The true story of the sculpture is that of the man behind it, one of Idaho’s early artists who witnessed the arc from a territory to a state. Charles Leopold Ostner is born in 1828 in Austria, formerly the Holy Roman Empire. As a student at Heidelberg University, the oldest and most prestigious university in now-modern Germany, he participates in the popular revolutions that sweep continental Europe in 1848 calling for democracy and constitutional governments. The revolutions’ failures and the subsequent repression by European monarchs contribute to high emigration to America. Ostner arrives at port in New Orleans in 1851, where he met another German emigrant by the name of Julia Armbruster. The pair are wed in 1852 and soon head west, to California, looking for gold. While Julia resides back at home in San Francisco, Charles has almost comically bad luck as a prospector as he travels up and down the western gold fields, including all the way up into Canada. There he hears about the discovery of gold by Capt. Elias Pierce in Washington Territory. He travels south to Lewiston and then on to fabulous Florence, but he instead becomes separated from the traveling party and is lost for days. (According to Hawley,) Packer John Welch finds Ostner unconscious and takes him to the camps at Florence where the other miners and pioneers help to nurse him back to health. The American Civil War is fully underway by now and the miners’ Union and Confederate sympathies cause tensions to run hot in the gold camps, especially as the intense snowfall precludes any further mining that winter and the men are largely confined to the saloons. Without informing them of his plan, Ostner recruits several men to assist him in collecting snow and hauling it to the stable. After the collected material reaches his specifications Ostner douses the snow in water, turning it into ice, and hides it behind canvas curtains. The other miners become curious about what he is up to, some even gambling about it. On the morning of February 22, 1863, Ostner pulls down the canvas curtains and fires his gun into the air, summoning the men to witness his creation: a life-sized ice sculpture of President George Washington, the father of the nation, gleaming in the morning sunlight. No gamblers guessed it right, so nobody wins or loses their bets, and the camp celebrates. Ostner retrieves the family, his wife Julia and their six children, from San Francisco in 1864 and moves them to Garden Valley, ID, where he tries and fails again at mining and ranching work. At the ranch homesite, he works a toll bridge over the South Fork of the Payette River. Ostner selects a massive yellow pine for his next carving project, another equestrian statue of Washington, but this time one that won’t melt. He writes to Gov. Edward Stevenson, offering the yet-to-be-carved gift to the Territory in memory of the first Idaho pioneers. Ranch life in the early Boise Basin was still difficult, leaving nights for Ostner to work on his Washington sculpture. His son Albert holds a torch for light, while his daughter Julia holds a stamp with the first president’s likeness on it when time comes to carve the head. It takes four years of work, including applying gold leaf from San Francisco, to complete it in 1869. The sculpture is loaded onto a sled and hauled to the travel road, then taken down to Boise. Ostner and his family move to Boise as well in 1869. The Territorial Legislature awards him $2,500 to show Idaho’s appreciation for the artwork. He continues traveling into old age. The sculpture of George Washington stands prominently outdoors in downtown Boise near the territorial capitol building, but the many years of exposure to the elements damages it. Some early Idaho historians claimed Ostner was not formally trained as an artist, but this is disproven by the oil paintings and woodcarvings and lithographs produced over his lifetime. They mostly feature horses, and/or depictions of Idaho’s people and locations of the day. The sculpture is moved to make way for construction of the state capitol building in 1905. Charles Ostner dies in 1913. His wife Julia dies in 1916. They are buried at Morris Hill. Their children and grandchildren are prominent Boiseans as the state matures further. State Treasurer John Eagleson taps a young Harry Hopffgarten in 1919 to see what can be done about the weathering and damage. Upon discovering dry rot in the wooden interior, he packs it with lead materials and patches it with help from cabinet maker William Gramkow. The sculpture is moved again in 1934, now placed inside the capitol building to avoid weathering. Political hijinks follow as elected officials feud over the exact placement. In 1966, capitol custodian E.T. Reeves notices damage to the statue (spurs broken off, etc.) which leads to another renovation campaign over several months, including a new glass case to prevent vandalism. Famed woodcarver Thayne Robertson carves the details that need replacement entirely. Hopffgarten, now age 83, is tapped again for the gold leaf work. For the bicentennial in 1976, locals in Garden Valley erect a monument at the home site. The statue is moved again for the capitol renovations in 2007-2010, including disassembly of the statue’s base which is then rebuilt with wood from trees removed from the grounds. It is cleaned and touched up again for the grand reopening and remains on the fourth floor. There are two versions of this tale that persist as the legend of Ostner fades: the first telling depicts him as just another random gold miner, untrained in the fine arts but overtaken with a patriotic spirit to produce this magnificent sculpture. The true story is that of a wandering artist from a family of Germanic woodcarvers who adopted brand-new Idaho as his muse. TIMELINE Ostner born in Austria-Germany 1828 Ostner attends University of Heidelberg Ostner involved in revolutions of 1848 Ostner meets Julia at New Orleans 1851 Ostner begins family in San Francisco 1852 Birth of daughter Emma in San Francisco 1858 Birth of son Albert in San Francisco 1858 Gold publicized in Idaho Territory ~1862 Ostner lost, rescued, carves ice sculpture Ostner moves family to Garden Valley 1864 Ostner fells tree and begins carving 1865 Ostner finishes the sculpture 1868 Ostner family moves to Boise 1869 Ostner bids on other statue jobs Ostner mining at Challis 1881 Death of daughter Emma in 1894 Ostner resides in Boise after 1900 Ostner dies, buried at Morris Hill 1913 Washington-Lincoln services 1915 Julia dies, buried at Morris Hill 1916 Statue weathering restored 1919 Statue moved indoors 1934 Statue restored again 1966 Monument erected at tree 1976 Capitol renovations 2007-2010
